extracted.intended_audience: researchers, postdocs, whistleblowers, and research-integrity stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating allegations of research misconduct in a lab: who is responsible, what institutional responses are expected, what evidence counts, and how community norms and incentives shape outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: PI ultimate responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “PI and PI only responsible for any fraud.” / “The PI is ultimately responsible for the research the emerges from the lab.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the principal investigator provided sufficient oversight; multiple problematic papers from a lab suggest PI-level failures (poor oversight, permissive culture, or direct participation). Distinguish single honest mistakes from systematic failures of supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual author accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: “The scientist who makes the mistake or commits the fraud is also responsible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When misconduct appears limited to a single paper or individual, assign primary blame to the responsible scientist, while still considering supervisory failures. Consider degrees of responsibility when personnel acted under instruction or coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/number-of-publications as indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: “What makes the Potti, Aggarwal, etc. cases so egregious is the number of publications at issue.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the quantity of suspect papers as a signal: many problematic papers amplify the likelihood of systemic misconduct, poor oversight, or entrenched culture; single instances more likely indicate isolated error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lab culture invites mistakes/fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: “a lab culture that invites mistakes/fraud” / descriptions of a “factory styled lab” producing redundant/low-quality papers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate working conditions (pressure to publish, unrealistic expectations, long hours) and whether they create incentives or cover for sloppy or fraudulent practices. Lab culture is a key factor in attributing systemic responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power dynamics and postdoc vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: “post docs are usually a vulnerable lot and more so when they are immigrants... on a visa” / “force a person to leave, use threats of canceling the visa.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for visa, employment, and hierarchical pressures that may coerce junior researchers into questionable practices. Vulnerability explains behavior but does not absolve misconduct; it should inform investigatory approaches and remedial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblowing timing and duty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Why no one informed earlier? In retrospect, do you think whistleblowing is a good thing? … this should have been done earlier…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timeliness of reports; earlier reporting can prevent further harm. Encourage clear channels and protections for whistleblowers; weigh motives but prioritize correcting the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional acknowledgement and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: “No acknowledgement whatsoever that he even received my emails. Not even a simple 'we’re looking into it' response.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should at minimum acknowledge receipt of complaints and indicate that an inquiry is underway, balancing confidentiality with accountability. Lack of acknowledgement is a red flag for institutional inaction or cover-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate oversight agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: References to ORI, FDA, and FOIA: “Any study in which the FDA was involved can be looked into by the FDA… FDA may have a few more teeth than the ORI… some of this information may be accessible under the FOIA.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct allegations to the jurisdictionally appropriate agency (institutional integrity office, ORI, FDA) and consider legal/public-record mechanisms (FOIA) when relevant. Different agencies have different powers and scopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t convict before investigation (presumption of innocence)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Have we forgotten in America you are innocent until proven guilty. The bloggers of this issue have taken upon themselves to be the judge and the jury without looking into all the facts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance public discussion with careful reliance on verified evidence. Avoid definitive public condemnation until formal investigation concludes, while still allowing community scrutiny to surface concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation and figure irregularities as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “look at the figures: apparently the Figure there are lots of irregularities ACTIN in C is looks like same and Figure F IKK alpha … flipped and stretched.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize images for duplication, flipping, stretching, or reuse across panels/experiments; documented image anomalies are concrete, testable indicators warranting formal inquiry and potential corrections/retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish error, negligence, and deliberate fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: “it will turn out to be ‘he did that’ vs ‘i was told to do that’ with the truth possibly somewhere in between”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intent and context: honest error, negligence, coercion, and intentional fabrication require different responses (correction, training/sanctions, institutional accountability, criminal/civil actions). Consider testimonies, patterns, and technical evidence to infer intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal responsibility to question data
rubrics_metrics.description: “The universities / institutes in India will investigate only if the Journal questions the data and asks them to... unlike in US where the journals majorly remain mute spectators.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect journals to play an active role in querying suspicious data, requesting raw data, and prompting institutional investigations. Evaluate whether journals acted appropriately in flagging concerns and issuing corrections/retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and clarity of corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: “I thought that a retraction and a withdrawal are the same thing. That is one of the problems of retractions: they go under different names.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear, consistent labeling and explanations for corrective actions (corrigendum, erratum, withdrawal, retraction) so readers understand the severity and scope of problems in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic incentives driving misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: “the blame should also go to the system. (dominance -grant, impact factor, publish or perish, and other such paraphernalia).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating misconduct, consider how funding pressures, impact-factor obsession, and career incentives may create perverse motivations. Remedies may need systemic reforms, not just individual punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate sanctions and remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: “This lab need to be closed down immediately, and all funding should be terminated.” / questions about whether wrongdoers will be punished or removed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend sanctions proportionate to findings: retractions, funding termination, employment consequences, or lab closure when systemic fraud is established. Consider both punitive and restorative remedies (corrections, training, policy changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative journalism and public exposure as a route
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions to pursue “investigative journalism and appropriate reporting and then write a book… Spicing up your research – title sounds good?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reporting and investigative journalism can surface patterns and pressure institutions to act, but should be fact-checked and responsible to avoid unfair defamation; combine public exposure with formal complaints to oversight bodies.
